name: Grace Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law, so it's lectures, a lot of case reading and a tutorial group where I say very little. I live in a flat share with two girls from my church youth group who also came to the city. On Saturdays I work at a garden centre, watering, lifting bags of compost and doing the till. My family has a small dairy farm two hours away, and the plan has always been that I come home and work for the solicitor in our market town, Mr Pryce, who knows my grandfather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. People get carried away with every new gadget, and the farm taught me that most things promised to make life easier mean new things to fix. I'd go to church on Sunday and not think about it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be at peace. The law is old and it moves slowly, and a solicitor in a market town is trusted because she's known. My worry is the farm: milk prices have been awful and Dad's been talking about selling the south field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on the same. Work Saturdays at the garden centre, read my cases the proper way with a pen and paper, and ask Mr Pryce whether I can shadow his office in the summer. I'd send some of my wages home, even a little, for the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quiet and grateful. I wouldn't be dancing about it, but there's relief. The worry about the farm is there in the background, like a tap dripping in another room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said milk prices are the real worry. What does that mean for you day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I don't ask for anything. I've never asked Mum for money for clothes, and I don't plan to. If the south field goes, I'd feel responsible, which isn't fair, but I'm the one with the education. I'd work extra at the garden centre in the summer rather than borrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the law offer you that you couldn't get another way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A place at home where people trust me. In our town you can't pretend. If you do a good job for a family, they remember for forty years, and if you don't, they remember that too. I want to be a person people go to when things go wrong.

say: I'd say most new gadgets just bring **new things to fix**.
I'd go to church and **not think** about it again.
think: Law moves slowly and a town solicitor is trusted because she's **known**.
My true worry is the **farm**, where Dad may sell the south field.
do: **Keep** the Saturday garden centre shifts and read cases with pen and paper.
**Ask** Mr Pryce if I can shadow his office in summer.
**Send** a little wage money home to the farm.
feel: **Quiet** and grateful, but not dancing about it.
The farm worry is like a **dripping tap** in another room.
S0.quote: I want to be a person people go to when things go wrong.
fieldNote: Her plan is a **return home**: the market-town solicitor who is known and trusted.
Real pressure is the family dairy farm's milk prices, not AI.
Feels responsible for the farm as the one with an education.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the garden centre
Send 40 a month of my wages to the farm
Ask Mr Pryce about shadowing his office in summer
Save the rest in a post office account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I'm sure it's clever but I don't see the need for it in a courtroom or a farm. I'd say people should keep their jobs for as long as they can do them well. And I'd say firms who throw out good staff for software will regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me more than I'd say. The first jobs for a law graduate are reading, checking and drafting, and those are exactly what the card says goes first. I don't want to be the girl whose training contract disappeared because a computer could do the filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to my way. Read the real books, learn to write a letter by hand, and go home in the summer to work with Mr Pryce, who isn't going to replace his staff with a computer. I'd stay away from the tools for now. I'd talk to my pastor and my parents, because I trust their judgment more than the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit hollow, like when the village post office closed. I feel it in my stomach on Sunday evenings when I think about Monday's lectures. It's not panic, it's more a dull ache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay away from the tools. Is that a risk for someone going into law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know it could be. But I've watched people trust a machine and not check it. If I'm slow at first, I'd rather be right. In a small town, the solicitor who knows the family and double-checks every date gets the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think should be done about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a lot from the government. I don't like handouts. I'd like firms to take on apprentices and trainees as they always did, and I'd like young people to be encouraged to learn a trade or a profession that needs hands and judgment. That's how my grandfather got started, and it worked.

say: I'd say firms that drop good staff for **software** will regret it.
I'd say people should keep jobs **as long as** they do them well.
think: The first jobs for law graduates are **reading and drafting**, which go first.
I fear my **training contract** disappearing because software does the filing.
do: **Stay away** from the tools for now and work with real books.
**Work** with Mr Pryce at home in the summer.
**Talk** to my parents and my pastor about the plan.
feel: **Hollow**, like when the village post office closed.
A **dull ache** on Sunday evenings, not panic.
S1.quote: In a small town, the solicitor who knows the family and double-checks every date gets the work.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** is rooted in values: caution, double-checking and trusting known people.
Dislikes handouts and wants firms to keep taking apprentices.
Sunday evening dread suggests more fear than she shows in public.

steps.text: Work summers in Mr Pryce's office back home
Talk to my parents and pastor about the plan
Hold off on the tools until others prove them
Offer the farm office a hand with paperwork at weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe a word of it and I'd pray about it. Two years is a very short time for anything. I'd say we have to keep faith and keep working, and I'd say it quietly so as not to frighten my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be very frightened. If everything a lawyer does can be done by a machine, my degree would be nothing, and Mr Pryce's office might close or shrink. The farm would still be there, since cows need milking until the robots arrive in 2031, but I'm not sure how long milk would pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home. I'd leave the degree if I had to and work on the farm, helping Dad with the books and the herd. I'd keep the garden centre job while I'm here, and send everything I earn home. I'd ask the church whether there's a fund for families who lose work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cold, sinking feeling. Like a long time ago, when the cows got sick and Dad didn't sleep. I'd be trying to look calm for my sister Ruth, who's 12.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might leave the degree. What would that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My place at the university and the future I planned. I'd feel I'd let my family down, because they were proud of me. But if the degree was worthless, leaving it early would save money. My grandmother says you don't keep paying for a roof that's fallen in, and the same goes for a degree that's worthless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight, over the kitchen table, after Sunday dinner, so they can't say I rushed it. I'd say I've looked at the facts, and I'd rather be at home helping than away running up a loan. Dad would argue, and Mum would cry, and then they'd agree. That's how our family works.

say: I'd say I **don't believe** it and I'd pray about it.
I'd say **quietly** that we must keep faith and keep working.
think: If a machine does a lawyer's work, my **degree** is worth nothing.
Mr Pryce's **office** might shrink, and milk may not pay for long.
do: **Go home** and work on the farm with Dad's books and herd.
**Send** everything I earn from the garden centre home.
**Ask** the church about a fund for families who lose work.
feel: A **cold, sinking** feeling, like when the cows got sick.
I'd try to look **calm** for my sister Ruth.
S2.quote: You don't keep paying for a roof that's fallen in, and the same goes for a degree that's worthless.
fieldNote: Her instinct is to **retreat home** to family and church, not to retrain.
Would leave the degree rather than run up debt, showing strong family duty.
Shows real fear behind her calm public line.

steps.text: Leave the degree if it stops making sense and go home
Help Dad with the farm books and the herd
Ask the church about a fund for affected families
Send all my garden centre wages home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so we shouldn't panic and we shouldn't ignore it. I'd say every family should have something that doesn't depend on a computer, like land or a skill with hands. I'd say that to my church group on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the end of my degree. I'd graduate in 2029, then maybe start work at Mr Pryce's in a world where the small jobs are changing. It's frightening but it isn't hopeless, because he'd know me and he'd keep me on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and do my training in a small firm, not a big city one. I'd learn the farm side too, like contracts and land law, so I'm useful at home in two ways. And I'd save about 40 a month in a savings account, nothing risky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Like a long walk home with weather coming in. You keep going, you keep an eye on the sky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every family should have something not dependent on a computer. What does yours have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Land, for as long as we can keep it. Milk, meat and vegetables. A decent kitchen and people who help each other. When I say that, I know it sounds old-fashioned. But if the cities have trouble, a farm family eats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the farm can't keep going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the south field before the house or the herd. And I'd use what I've learnt in law to help with the sale and the paperwork, because I'd rather my father trusted me than a stranger. That would be one good use of the degree, at least.

say: I'd say every family needs something that doesn't depend on a **computer**.
I'd say that to my **church group** on Sunday.
think: Five years is the **end of my degree**, in a world changing small jobs.
Mr Pryce would **know me** and keep me on.
do: **Finish** the degree and train at a small firm, not a city one.
**Learn** contract and land law so I'm useful on the farm.
**Save** 40 a month in a plain savings account.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, like walking home with weather coming in.
I **keep going** and watch the sky.
S3.quote: If the cities have trouble, a farm family eats.
fieldNote: Sees **land and family** as her security, which is a traditional answer.
Plans to make her law degree useful at home in two ways.
Mood stays anxious because her path into law is shaky and the farm's income is thin.

steps.text: Finish the degree and train at a small firm
Take land and contract law modules for the farm
Save 40 a month in a plain savings account
Keep working Saturdays at the garden centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and most of us will be doing what we do now for most of it. I'd tell my friends to carry on, be kind, and not stop trying. I'd also say that a decade is time for the country to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I could be a solicitor with eight years' experience by 2036, with a settled place at home. I might even be married, with a child of my own. That feels a long way off, but it's what I've always wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, train at the market town firm, and buy a little house near the farm. I'd learn the tools a few years in, if people I trusted said they were safe. And I'd keep going to church and keeping my own accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A plain, ordinary sort of calm, like a Sunday afternoon. I'd still say a prayer for the people who'd lose out, but I'd be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools if people you trust say they're safe. Who would those people be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Pryce, my tutor and maybe my cousin who's a vet. Not strangers on the internet. If those three said, we use it and it saves time, I'd try it. I'm not against the tools forever, I just don't see why I should be the first one in the water.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your family in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's time to get the farm on a more secure footing. Maybe a farm shop, or letting the south field to a neighbour. Ten years gives us room to think. With 2028 I'd just be panicking, but here Dad and I can sit down and make a plan together.

say: I'd say ten years means most of us will keep **doing** what we do now.
I'd tell friends to **be kind** and keep trying.
think: By 2036 I could be a **solicitor** with eight years' experience at home.
A decade is enough for the **country** to get ready.
do: **Finish** the degree and train at the market town firm.
**Buy** a little house near the farm.
**Try** the tools only after trusted people vouch for them.
feel: I'd **pray** for those who lose out, but I'd be okay.
S4.quote: I'm not against the tools forever, I just don't see why I should be the first one in the water.
fieldNote: Time lets her **soften** her stance within her trusted circle.
Her family plan becomes constructive: a farm shop, not a retreat.
Calm is sincere and rooted in home and faith.

steps.text: Finish the degree and train at the market town firm
Plan a farm shop with Dad on the south field
Try the tools once Mr Pryce says they're safe
Save for a deposit on a house near the farm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there'd be no time to plan and I'd have to make hard choices about my degree and about the farm. What would help is families and churches being ready to look after each other, and firms still taking on trainees. I don't want a government cheque, but I'd want a fair chance to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think I'm behind because I don't use these things. I'm not behind, I'm careful, and I'd like to be asked what I want from the future. Not just what I think of the machine.

headlineQuote: I'm not behind, I'm careful, and I'd like to be asked what I want from the future.
portrait: Grace is an **18-year-old** law student from a small dairy farm, who works Saturdays at a garden centre.
Her **traditional** outlook centres on family, church and a plan to be a trusted solicitor in her home town.
She is **resistant** to AI, trusts people she knows and prefers firms to keep training apprentices over government handouts.
Her **money** worry is the farm: milk prices, and the chance her father sells the south field.
She is uneasy in the quiet world, alarmed by 2028 and thinking of home, then calm with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to plan for her degree or the farm.
whatWouldHelp: Families and **churches** ready to look after each other.
Firms that still **take on trainees**, giving young people a fair chance to work.
